speaker: Jeff Currie
title: Jeff Currie on the 'Volatility Trap' Keeping Commodity Prices So High
question: In commodity trading, why do financially intermediated long-term contracts break down during price spikes unlike traditional direct supply agreements?
guest: In the '70s, we did this with conglomerates and long-term contracts. If somebody failed a long-term contract, it would be resolved in a court of law. Then in the 2000s, the banks got in between these conglomerates—say between a GM and an Alcoa—to squeeze in there and provide a lower cost of capital. You had the financial market squeeze in there and create a new kind of long-term contract that was financially based. Now, the problem with that is when you go through periods like we are right now and the price of that long-term contract goes up because it's traded on the market, you get a huge capital call and a margin call, which is what was happening in that case in nickel. Then you need the cash to fund that margin call. You didn't have that back in the '70s; you have it today. So the question is whether we gravitate back closer to the '70s to deal with this problem, or try to fix the structure created in the 2000s, which means you're going to need different types of lending agreements.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Financially intermediated contracts break down in price spikes mainly because they are collateralized and marked to market, whereas traditional direct supply agreements rest on bilateral credit and a physical relationship.

When a producer or trader hedges through futures, cleared swaps, or bank-intermediated deals, a price spike generates immediate variation margin calls on short positions, and exchanges raise initial margins as volatility climbs. The hedger's offsetting gain, the physical commodity it will deliver later, is illiquid and unrealized, so a firm that is economically hedged can still run out of cash. Banks financing those positions hit credit limits and pull back just when funding needs peak. This forces position liquidations, defaults, or bailouts, as seen with European energy utilities in 2022, the LME nickel squeeze, and Metallgesellschaft in 1993.

A direct supplier-buyer contract has no daily cash settlement: the loss is an opportunity cost realized gradually at delivery, and both sides have relationship and reputational incentives to renegotiate rather than terminate.

Intermediation also adds a party with strong incentives to default or exploit termination clauses when spot prices far exceed contract prices.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Traditional direct supply agreements pair producers and end-users with naturally offsetting physical positions: producers own the underlying reserves, buyers need the physical input, and payments settle gradually upon delivery without daily mark-to-market collateralization. Sunk investments in dedicated infrastructure and long-term bilateral ties further deter breach when spot prices surge.

Financially intermediated contracts replace captive physical backing with leveraged balance sheets and dynamic derivatives hedging, creating acute liquidity, basis, and incentive mismatches during price spikes. Because intermediaries hedge long-term commitments with futures or cleared swaps—often rolling shorter-dated positions—a sudden price spike triggers massive immediate cash margin calls, whereas offsetting physical contract cash flows arrive only upon future delivery. Simultaneously, extreme backwardation and basis blowouts erode imperfect hedges, forcing intermediaries to buy scarce spot supply or liquidate hedges at steep losses. Lacking owned production and deep relational lock-in, intermediaries face severe funding squeezes or incentives for opportunistic default when capped non-delivery penalties fall below spot windfalls.

noweb.answer: Financially intermediated long-term contracts break down during commodity price spikes primarily due to acute liquidity mismatches and margin mechanics absent from traditional direct supply agreements. Intermediaries typically hedge long-term physical commitments using exchange-traded derivatives marked to market daily. When prices surge, these short hedges trigger immediate, massive variation margin calls, whereas offsetting cash inflows from physical deliveries materialize only gradually over years. Even when the overall position remains economically sound at maturity, this sudden cash drain can exhaust credit lines, forcing intermediaries to liquidate hedges at peak losses or default. Because intermediaries also lack underlying production assets and frequently roll short-dated futures, they face severe basis and rollover risks during physical squeezes, alongside lower reputational costs for defaulting on purely transactional deals. By contrast, traditional bilateral agreements link physical producers and end-users directly without daily margining. Anchored by actual commodity output, dedicated infrastructure, and mutual operational dependence, direct counterparties possess natural physical hedges and strong relational incentives to fulfill or renegotiate contracts through extreme volatility rather than walk away.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Long-term contracts that run through financial intermediaries usually depend on hedges that are marked to market. A trader or bank that sells a fixed-price contract to a utility or manufacturer offsets the risk on exchanges or with other dealers. When prices spike, those hedges lose value on paper and the intermediary must post cash as variation margin, often daily, long before the physical contract delivers its offsetting gain. The underlying position can be economically sound and still fail for lack of cash. Firms then cut credit lines, close out positions, or default, and contracts unwind exactly when buyers need them. Europe's energy crisis in 2022 and the LME nickel squeeze that year both showed this.

Direct supply agreements between a producer and a consumer usually aren't marked to market. They rely on credit, renegotiation clauses, and the long-term relationship. A producer may lose money compared with the spot price, but it doesn't face a sudden cash call, and walking away would damage its reputation and future business. So the contract can bend to absorb the spike instead of forcing liquidation.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Financially intermediated long-term contracts, routed through exchanges, clearinghouses, or banks, break down during price spikes because they decouple financial settlement from physical delivery and require daily mark-to-market margining. When prices surge, a producer or merchant who hedged future supply via short derivatives faces immediate cash variation margin calls, compounded by procyclical hikes in initial margin as volatility climbs. Although the firm remains economically solvent because its future physical output has risen in value by an offsetting amount, that output will not generate cash until delivery. Since financial intermediaries rarely accept physical reserves or future production as collateral, this timing mismatch triggers an acute liquidity squeeze, forcing solvent participants to exhaust credit lines, unwind hedges at a loss, or default. By contrast, traditional direct supply agreements are bilateral and unmargined: no interim cash changes hands as spot prices move, physical delivery naturally settles the obligation, and extreme stress is managed through bilateral credit or renegotiation rather than automated collateral calls.

noweb.answer:
Financially intermediated long-term contracts break down during price spikes primarily because they replace delivery-based settlement with daily mark-to-market collateralization. Intermediaries such as banks and trading houses hedge their exposure with exchange-traded futures or cleared swaps. When prices surge, the short side faces immediate cash margin calls even though the offsetting gain on the physical commodity will not be realized until future delivery. This liquidity mismatch can exhaust credit lines and trigger forced liquidation or default, whereas traditional direct supply agreements typically settle upon physical delivery without daily cash drains.

Furthermore, intermediaries operate under strict balance-sheet, risk, and capital limits that tighten abruptly during extreme volatility. Widening basis risk between financial benchmarks and physical delivery, alongside rising counterparty credit concerns, often compels them to unwind hedges or pull credit. By contrast, direct producer-to-consumer agreements rest on mutual operational dependence, giving both sides strong incentives to ride out temporary paper losses or renegotiate rather than terminate.

A price spike can turn a financially intermediated long-term contract into an immediate cash problem. The intermediary may have to post variation margin on a futures hedge today, while payment on the offsetting contract arrives months later. Even if the two positions offset economically, the intermediary can run out of cash or credit and be forced to close the hedge or default. A cash-settled hedge also leaves the buyer responsible for finding the commodity.

Under a traditional fixed-price supply agreement, the producer can usually meet its obligation by delivering from its own output. If it can deliver, the higher spot price is mainly a forgone opportunity to sell at a higher price. The agreement typically requires no daily cash payment for that difference. Direct contracts can still fail if the producer loses output and has to buy replacement supply at the higher spot price.

A price spike can leave a financially intermediated contract sound on paper but short of cash. Suppose an intermediary agrees to buy a commodity at a fixed price for future delivery and sells futures to hedge that purchase. When prices spike, the right to buy cheaply becomes more valuable, but the intermediary must post cash immediately to cover losses on the futures. If it exhausts its credit before the commodity arrives, it may have to unwind the hedge or default.

In a traditional direct supply agreement, the producer can usually fulfill the same fixed-price promise by delivering the commodity. The spike raises the profit the producer forgoes by honoring the deal, but it typically creates no immediate margin call. Direct agreements can still fail, especially if a producer cannot deliver. The distinctive risk in the intermediated deal is that cash can come due well before the offsetting gain can be realized.
